column3: Closest parallel: combat, turning backs, and then no aid occur in one sequence.
Adds the category of harmful speech, but not the conflict outcome.
Contrasts claimed agents with any independent power to harm or benefit.
Directly parallels the combat conditional, retreat, and absence of helper.
The next ayah develops the hostile group's imposed abasement and dependence.
Its no-harm/no-benefit contrast is distant from the military scene.
Sets turning backs in battle as the central opposed action.
The immediate passage qualifies hostile plotting as unable to harm under patience and taqwa.
Shows harm exposing dependence, without the adversarial reversal.
Distinguishes actual combat from withdrawal and peace in a conflict setting.
Uses turning backs to depict failed reception, a secondary retreat image.
Reflection on the Book does not clarify limited harm or defeat.
Limits the relevant conflict category to those who fight or expel.
The nearby context supplies support amid an approaching attack.
Face-and-back blows are punitive imagery, not battlefield withdrawal.
Supplies a reciprocal combat condition, but not the promised defeat.

Explicitly denies both aid to others and self-aid.
Places injury within changing communal fortunes rather than decisive finality.
Makes harm and benefit a test of claimed agency, only indirectly relevant.
Ends a leadership trajectory with no aid, but lacks the battle reversal.
The summons to mutual invocation does not add to the stated outcome.
States that hostile private talk cannot harm except by permission.
Pairs the failure of plotting with the absence of aid.

Denies personal ownership of harm, qualifying who controls outcomes.
Directly states that allied parties cannot avail or aid one another.
The account of Mary does not clarify the focus.
Constrains harmful effects by permission, but the subject matter is remote.
Defines a form of adhā, though not the target's limited hostile harm.
Continues the guidance-and-retreat image without the outcome of defeat.
Uses the same no-harm formula to show that refusal rebounds on its agents.
Contrasts giving that does not follow with adhā, clarifying the word's social use.
Provision for Mary does not bear on harm, combat, or aid.
A harmful false protector is only a distant contrast to failed support.
Repeats the no-harm formula with an explicitly different object: God.
Respite and a firm plan do not materially clarify the focus.
Denies harm-benefit power to objects of worship, outside the conflict claim.
Nearby context names abundant adhā and answers it with patience and taqwa.
Mortality and final success do not add to the stated battlefield reversal.
Denies ownership of harm and benefit, a secondary authority contrast.
Mentions inconvenience amid combat precautions but not limited hostile harm.
Face-and-back punishment is a distinct, final scene.
The garment evidence scene does not elucidate turning backs in combat.
Questions whether plotting can remove the anger surrounding divine support.
Provides the false advance promise of combat support fulfilled negatively in 59:12.
Rejects appeals to what can neither benefit nor harm.
Identifies adhā as a concrete condition requiring restraint, not decisive injury.
Forced faces in the Fire are only a remote orientation reversal.
Differentiated reward for struggle does not clarify this defeat claim.
The limited-days claim about the Fire is unrelated.
Names causing harm to the messenger, but not the focus's outcome.
Removal of harm and continued rebellion are not the battle sequence.
Establishes that no one removes harm except God.
Denies any protector or helper apart from God.
The response to relief after distress does not clarify the conflict outcome.
The limited-days assertion does not add to 3:111.
Mutual repudiation ends with no helpers, but in a different scene.
The flight and garment evidence scene is not the target's military reversal.
Exile and destruction of an idol do not add to the focus.
Exposes those who claim alliance after promised support, under pressure.
The no-harm claim is redirected to God and followed by ruined deeds.
The writing and non-harm rule for contracts is unrelated.
Gradual drawing on does not clarify limited harm or no aid.
Denies reciprocal control of benefit and harm among the assembled parties.
Hardship functions as pressure toward supplication, not hostile defeat.
The appointed meeting with God does not add to the focus.
Rearward following and no looking back form a different departure scene.
The directional garment evidence is unrelated to the target's reversal.
Testing truthfulness does not clarify harm, retreat, or aid.
Denies even the messenger's independent control over harm and benefit.
Supplies a contrary case where hostile dominance would bring severe coercion.
The call at the fire does not add to the focus.
Reflection on discourse is not an added reading of 3:111.
Links reliance on wrongdoers to harm, absence of protectors, then no aid.
A sudden backward flight supplies a secondary image of retreat.
Tests alleged agents by whether they can remove or retain harm and mercy.
Self-purification does not clarify the target.
The distress-relief cycle does not add to the battlefield claim.
The rejection of other lords does not materially clarify 3:111.
Depicts retreating backs with no protector from God.
Denies that flight from death or killing brings benefit.
Its legal and ritual provisions do not add to the focus.
Distinguishes withdrawal, peace, and renewed hostile action in conflict.
Economic distress and appeal for charity are unrelated.
Names hostile hands and tongues, sharpening the limited adhā side of the focus.
Denies alleged agents power to remove or redirect harm.
Makes not turning backs an accountable covenant, directly opposing the predicted retreat.
Denies personal ownership of harm and benefit, including the messenger's own case.
What is unseen does not add to the focus.
Ritual purification and hardship relief are unrelated.
Taking a false ally leads to misguidance and punishment, not the stated reversal.
The distress-and-association cycle does not clarify 3:111.
The doctrinal warning does not add to limited harm or failed aid.
The facial reaction supplies no material link.
The divine attributes alone do not sharpen the focus.
Easy accounting does not add to the target.

Begins the surrounding battle sequence by positioning believers for combat.
Shows two groups nearing loss of resolve while God is their protector.
Names divine help at Badr, supplying the positive counterpart to no aid.
Continues the immediate support scene with promised reinforcements.
States that help belongs to God alone, grounding the final no-aid clause.
Describes the hostile side being cut down or turned back disappointed.
Forbids loss of resolve and grief, a nearby contrast to retreat.
Links battle disorder and turning away to a failed response under pressure.
Directly states that none can overcome when God helps, and none can help when He forsakes.
Counters a claim that obedience could have prevented killing, but not the stated reversal.
Shows believers responding after injury rather than being overcome by it.
Turns a threat of gathered forces into reliance on God's sufficiency.
Denies the adversary's power over the faithful and redirects fear to God.
Frames fighting under the way of God through exchange of worldly life.
Makes fighting a response to oppressed people seeking rescue.
Contrasts fighting under God with fighting under false powers and calls their scheme weak.
Records the believers' call for aid and its answer with reinforcements.
Defines reinforcement as reassurance and locates help with God alone.
Directly regulates turning one's back in battle and distinguishes it from tactical movement.
States that God weakens the plot of the disbelievers.
Ties the sought decision to the defeated party's cessation and threat of return.
Commands steadfastness and remembrance upon meeting a force.
Warns that dispute produces failure and loss of strength.
Depicts a promised guarantee of non-defeat collapsing into backward flight and disavowal.
Makes a decisive encounter scatter those behind the hostile party.
Orders combat as a means of breaking hostile power and bringing relief to believers.
Recalls a day when numerical strength did not avail and the earth constricted.
Follows retreat with divine tranquility, reinforcements, and punishment of deniers.
Shows divine aid arriving when human companionship offers no material support.
Limits what can befall believers to what God has decreed and names Him protector.
Defines believing men and women as mutual protectors, a positive aid relation.
Authorizes those fought because they were wronged and affirms divine power to aid them.
Promises support to those who support God and identifies Him as strong and mighty.
Recalls hostile forces being repelled by divine wind and unseen forces.
Presents a call to flee when a group claims it has no secure position.
Portrays hostile confederates as still imagining the parties have not departed.
States that God turned back the disbelievers in rage without their gaining good.
Depicts the hostile group being brought down from fortified positions.
Sets the battle encounter within a sequence ending in the weakening of disbelievers.
Promises that supporting God brings divine support and firm footing.
Forbids calling for peace from weakness while God is with believers.
Names a mighty divine help, the positive ground beneath the target's denial of aid.
Locates the forces of heaven and earth with God and names His might.
Promises believers gains and restrains hostile hands from them.
Presents the divine pattern that leaves no alternative to God's way.
Shows a protected group expelled from homes through an unexpected divine action.
Explains the hostile group's fear as greater than fear of God.
Says their apparent collective strength is divided internally, qualifying any promise of support.
Pairs promised victory with a near opening, adding an explicit support horizon.
Names God, Gabriel, and the righteous believers as supporters against opposition.
